summary.text: A cover page giving the title Handbook for Guideline Development, 2nd edition, followed by the start of the cataloguing-in-publication notice.

Carries the publication front matter for the handbook: cataloguing data, acknowledgements naming the author, contributors, reviewers and funder, the copyright and disclaimer notices, and the full table of contents for the chapters. It then gives the foreword, which says the second edition adds more detailed guidance on each step plus two new chapters, one on equity, human rights, gender and social determinants and one on rapid advice guidelines in public health emergencies. The foreword also states that the guidance will be updated as methods evolve and invites feedback to the guideline review secretariat.

Defines a WHO guideline as any WHO document containing recommendations for clinical practice or public health policy. Explains that a recommendation tells the intended user what to do in specific situations to achieve the best health outcomes and helps users decide, select and prioritize among interventions.

Explains that WHO develops guidelines when Member States, country offices, experts or other stakeholders ask for guidance because they are unsure what to do. Lists the triggers of such uncertainty: a new problem or emergency, new evidence, a lack of good evidence, or a change in resources or access to services.

Describes the principle that WHO is a science- and evidence-based organization, citing its general programme of work. States that guidelines are the main means of exercising technical leadership and that WHO's authority rests on systematic use of evidence.

Lists the principles WHO guidelines must follow, after noting that WHO uses internationally recognized methods and standards. The principles include addressing a real area of uncertainty, reflecting the right to health, transparent and explicit development, multidisciplinary input, minimizing bias, systematic weighing of benefits and harms, public availability of evidence, adaptability to local settings, and tailoring to a specific audience.

sections.title: What is the aim of this handbook?

summary.text: States the aim of the handbook: to set out principles and stepwise instruction for developing a WHO guideline. Says the goal is a credible guideline whose recommendations balance benefits and harms, meet WHO publication standards, rest on accessible evidence and can be implemented to benefit population health.

sections.title: For whom is this handbook intended?

summary.text: Lists the intended readers of the handbook: WHO staff and departments wishing to produce a guideline, members of the steering, development and external review groups, and anyone wanting to understand how WHO develops guidelines.
Says the handbook follows guideline development from deciding whether a guideline is needed through to publication, and points to a table summarizing the process and its main contributors.

Explains that the type of guideline determines methods, resources and time frame, and that types differ in purpose, scope, timing, developer, new versus existing recommendations and timeline. Names four main types (standard, consolidated, interim, and emergency or urgent-need) plus other less frequent types. Presents a table of the development process by stage, contributor, step and chapter, from planning through publishing and updating, and a table comparing each type's purpose, scope, developer, recommendations and development period.

Describes standard guidelines, which cover a clinical or policy area and can range from a single drug to the full scope of a condition, with recommendations either new or updated. Lists their usual focus areas such as clinical interventions, health-system policy, public health exposures, diagnostic tests and surveillance, and states they typically take 9 to 24 months, need systematic reviews and one or two group meetings, and have a review date. Notes that most WHO guidelines are of this type.

Defines a consolidated guideline as a compilation of recommendations from existing WHO guidelines or from other organizations' guidelines produced by consistent processes. Explains that it is complex to produce and maintain, that all included recommendations must be up to date and approved by the review committee, and that cross-referencing is required. Sets out when committee review is needed and the one case in which it is not.

Describes interim guidelines, produced when guidance is requested while data are incomplete, for example for a new intervention, disease or data. Says they have a narrow scope and short shelf-life, must state when more evidence is expected, and still comply fully with the handbook's processes and standards despite pressure for speed.

sections.title: Guidelines in response to an emergency or urgent need

summary.text: Describes guidelines produced for emergencies or urgent need and distinguishes two basic kinds. Emergency (rapid response) guidelines may rely on existing guidelines or expert opinion within hours to days but must still keep basic quality principles and document their rationale. Rapid advice guidelines follow WHO processes more closely, carry a review-by date and need committee review at both stages. Also notes that urgent recommendations outside an emergency must rest on a systematic review and meet all handbook standards.

sections.title: Additional types of guidelines produced by WHO
Guidelines developed in collaboration with external organizations

summary.text: Explains how WHO may jointly produce guidelines with external organizations, which must still follow WHO's basic principles. Lists requirements including no commercial funding, managed conflicts of interest, a systematic review, transparent methods, representative experts and consultation on publishing. States that staff must submit a planning proposal highlighting any deviation, which the review committee assesses case by case.

Covers guidelines developed by external organizations that WHO might adopt, adapt or incorporate, which requires careful evaluation of quality and applicability. Says such guidelines rarely meet two standards, global applicability and expert panels representing all WHO regions, so adoption is rare. Specifies what the planning proposal for an endorsed or adapted guideline must contain.

Explains that WHO guidelines made for one setting may be adapted to another, for example routine obstetric care adapted for emergency settings. States that adaptations follow standard review-committee procedures and that further guidance on adapting in urgent situations is being developed.

sections.title: Information products that are not considered guidelines

summary.text: Lists document types that are not considered guidelines and need no committee review, such as statements of established principles, governing-body reports, purely informational documents, manufacturing standards, operational how-to manuals and standard operating procedures. Advises consulting the committee secretariat when unsure.

Describes the Guideline Review Committee, established by the Director-General in 2007 to ensure WHO guidelines are high quality, transparently developed and evidence-based. Says it has about 30 members from all WHO regions plus external members and meets monthly.

sections.title: Terms of reference of the GRC

summary.text: Sets out the committee's terms of reference: it must approve all WHO publications containing recommendations and reviews each guideline twice, at the planning stage and after the final document is edited. Explains what each review checks, that the committee advises on process and methods but not technical content, and how its approval fits into WHO's internal clearance sequence.

Lists the roles of the review committee secretariat, which supports the committee, advises WHO staff, sets benchmarks and evaluates guideline processes for quality assurance. Itemizes its tasks, including coordinating technical support, organizing training, collaborating with methodological networks and keeping a database of submissions.

A numbered list of six references for Chapter 1, covering the general programme of work, the WHO Constitution, the committee's establishment note and WHO manual and intranet pages. The extraction also includes the opening sentence of Chapter 2 on the value of early planning.

Opens the question of whether a guideline is really needed, noting that development is time-consuming and expensive and that requests exceed capacity. Advises asking key questions before deciding to proceed.
Asks whether Member States have requested the guideline, noting that WHO guidelines should generally meet global or regional needs and take a public health perspective.

sections.title: Should WHO be the organization to produce this guideline?

summary.text: Poses questions on whether governing bodies requested the guideline and whether WHO is best placed to issue guidance on the topic; the text breaks off mid-sentence because of the page split.

Mixes the end of the question on whether WHO should produce a guideline, which refers to its resources, implementation skills and local knowledge, with the section on whether guidelines on the topic already exist. Advises consulting WHO departments, the review committee secretariat and the library to avoid duplication, and examining or updating existing guidelines that are out of date.

sections.title: What purpose and audience does the guideline serve?

summary.text: Introduces the section on purpose and audience, stating that staff need a clear goal and audience in mind when developing a guideline.

Poses questions about what a guideline will achieve, such as addressing poor practice or changing programmes or policy while fulfilling the right to health. States that resolving users' uncertainty should be the focus of most guidelines.

sections.title: What are the specific objectives of the guideline?

summary.text: Asks what health indicators, tests or approaches a guideline targets and says clear, achievable objectives will govern and facilitate its development.

States that a guideline needs a clearly defined target audience identified early, with recommendations tailored to it. Clarifies that end-users apply the guideline while recipients receive the interventions, and warns against writing for policy-makers, managers and clinicians at once.

sections.title: Who are the recipients of the interventions?

summary.text: Asks who the service users and other recipients of the recommended interventions are, and says their perspectives and needs must be built into guideline development from the beginning.
Says the best start time and the completion time frame for a guideline must be considered carefully at the outset.

Asks whether now is the best time to develop recommendations, given expected new data or changes in infrastructure or policy that could affect implementation. Also says the timeline must match when guidance is needed, with a narrow high-quality standard guideline taking at least 9 to 12 months and a broad one with many new systematic reviews taking 2 to 3 years.

sections.title: Is the guideline a response to a situation calling for urgent advice?

summary.text: Explains that a guideline responding to urgent advice needs different processes and methods, often a greatly reduced scope. Warns that rapid methods carry a high risk of bias, which staff must balance against the demand for speed, and refers to Chapter 11.

sections.title: Will the recommendations in the guideline be implemented?

summary.text: States that guidelines aim to improve health and therefore must be disseminated, adopted or adapted, and implemented. Introduces the question of whether recommendations will actually be implemented.

sections.title: Are the guideline and its implementation within the relevant programme’s work area and budget?

summary.text: Explains that under WHO reform all work must fall within the General Programme of Work and Programme Budget, so a guideline outside that remit will be hard to justify in resources and budget.

sections.title: Is a process for disseminating and implementing the recommendations in place?

summary.text: Poses questions about who will implement the recommendations, what level and format of guidance is needed, and what infrastructure, services and access are required. Says these issues should be considered from the start because they affect who is involved, resources and how recommendations are written.

sections.title: Who should be involved in developing a guideline?

summary.text: Says guideline development involves many groups and people, referring to Chapter 3, and that they should be engaged from the outset.

sections.title: Do you have your director’s agreement?

summary.text: States that the director's formal approval is needed before the planning proposal or final guideline goes to the review committee, and that the assistant director-general must approve the final guideline afterwards.

sections.title: What WHO departments must be involved?

summary.text: Asks which other headquarters and regional departments, including those with cross-cutting mandates, have interest, expertise or similar products. Advises preparing a list of WHO technical units and external organizations, experts and stakeholders to consult.

sections.title: Have you identified experts in guideline methods?

summary.text: Says WHO staff usually commission experts in systematic reviews and guideline development to help with key questions, evidence work and turning evidence into recommendations, and that they should be identified early.
Introduces further factors to consider once a guideline is judged needed by its end-users and beneficial to recipients, before starting the project.

sections.title: Do you have the necessary resources to develop a guideline?

summary.text: Asks whether resources are sufficient for systematic reviews, meetings and production costs. Notes that WHO cannot use commercial money for guidelines and that development demands long hours from staff.

sections.title: What publication types and formats are you considering?

summary.text: Advises considering the level of detail and format that users want, and budgeting for derivative products such as summaries, algorithms or wall charts, since users rarely want detail on methods. Suggests electronic versions with short paper publications may be cheaper and more practical.
Asks which languages are spoken by those most in need of the advice and says to weigh translation implications for budget and timeline when choosing languages.

Defines scoping as deciding what a guideline will and will not include, and lists what must be determined: areas of practice or policy, interventions or exposures, affected populations and important benefit and harm outcomes. Explains that scoping sets the focus and key questions and keeps the guideline manageable, and calls it one of the hardest and most important steps because a wrong scope wastes resources and leaves users uncertain.

Lists the steps of scoping, coordinated by the responsible technical officer: draft the scope, set up the steering group, refine priority topics, run a preliminary literature search, keep the topic list minimal, and formulate key questions in the population, intervention, comparator and outcome format. Stresses avoiding a textbook-style scope, focusing on areas of desired change, inequity, controversy or uncertainty, and considering equity, human rights and gender early.

Despite its heading, contains the closing steps of the scoping procedure: circulating a scope summary to the development group and other stakeholders while reminding them that a guideline is not a textbook, and then reconsidering feasibility, time frame and resources after feedback.

Begins with a single reference on WHO reform, then opens Chapter 3 by naming the four groups to be established: the steering group, the guideline development group, the external review group and the systematic review team. Describes the steering group's composition, size and time commitment, and lists its roles, from drafting the scope and managing conflicts of interest to organizing meetings, drafting the guideline, overseeing review and publication, and monitoring the need for updates.

Describes the guideline development group as external experts who develop evidence-based recommendations and finalize the scope and key questions. Explains when it is established, how members are chosen for skills, diversity and geography, the usual size of 10 to 20, and that it normally needs at least one face-to-face meeting.

sections.title: Contributors and their role in guideline development

summary.text: Despite its heading, describes the development group's terms of participation and role: members are not paid beyond expenses and act as individuals rather than representatives of their institutions. Lists the group's roles, including giving input on scope, ranking outcomes, examining evidence profiles, interpreting benefits and harms, and formulating recommendations.

sections.title: Composition of the guideline development group

summary.text: Explains how the development group should be composed: multidisciplinary, balanced by gender and geography, excluding WHO and UN staff, and screened for conflicts of interest. Describes member types and their value, including the chair and vice-chair or co-chairs, technical experts, end-users, representatives of affected people with the benefits of and barriers to service-user involvement, methods experts, an economist and an equity, human rights and gender expert.

Describes the external review group of interested people and stakeholders, including experts, end-users, programme managers and affected individuals, and how and when the steering group establishes it. Says it should be balanced and may review the scope, key questions and the final guideline, where its role is to find errors, comment on clarity and implementation, and not to change recommendations.

Explains that systematic reviews underpin most recommendations and are usually commissioned from external contractors with no financial conflicts, identified early, with the Cochrane and Campbell collaborations as possible sources. Then presents a multi-page table summarizing each contributing group, covering its responsibilities, functions, timing, establishment, leaders, expertise, size and whether declarations of interest are required, down to observers and funders.

sections.title: Other individuals and groups involved in guideline development

summary.text: A heading page for the section on other individuals and groups involved in guideline development, with no body text.

Explains that at least one methodologist, an expert in guideline processes, systematic reviews, GRADE and turning evidence into recommendations, should be involved. Says they should be identified early to help with planning and key questions and should help the development group formulate recommendations transparently at meetings.

Describes commissioned consultants with additional expertise such as modelling, economics or epidemiology, who may present at group meetings. States that they do not contribute to formulating recommendations unless they are official members of the development group.

sections.title: Observers at the meeting of the guideline development group

summary.text: Explains that stakeholders such as nongovernmental organizations, advocacy groups, funders and service users may be invited to send observers to development group meetings. Observers do not take part in formulating recommendations, though the chair may ask for their information.

Explains that one designated writer or editor should draft and finalize the guideline, incorporating group and peer-review comments. Says the writer should be involved from planning, attend meetings, know the WHO style guide and consult equity, human rights and gender experts on how people are described.

States that funders can play no role in development and must not influence recommendations. Private funders may observe meetings but not contribute to reviews or recommendations, while governmental and intergovernmental funders may partner, with their employees in the steering group but not the development group unless the dual role is declared and managed as a conflict of interest.

sections.title: Identifying and managing conflicts of interest

summary.text: Points to Chapter 6 and the compliance office for how conflicts of interest are identified and managed, and says declarations are collected before appointments and later changes reported to the steering group. States that major conflicts bar appointment while minor ones can be managed individually or at group level. Also begins the section on managing an effective group meeting, with the steering group and chair responsible.

sections.title: The role of the chair and vice-chair

summary.text: Describes the chair's duties at meetings: letting members present views, keeping to the agenda, summarizing opinions, raising relevant issues and steering the group to consensus. Says the chair and vice-chair should not impose their opinions, though they may state them in a personal capacity.

sections.title: Decision-making in the guideline development group

summary.text: Says the steering group must plan how the development group will make decisions, agreed with the chair and vice-chair before the first meeting and presented there. States that groups should generally decide by consensus, that acceptable approaches and a fallback if consensus fails must be defined in advance.

Explains that most guidelines need at least one face-to-face meeting of the development group, sometimes preceded by one to settle scope and key questions. Says the steering group must make sure attendees understand how the meeting runs, their roles and the expected outputs.

Lists questions the steering group should consider when planning a meeting, covering its purpose, specific objectives, decisions that need not involve the group, and the decisions and outputs expected.

Lists questions on preparing for a meeting: how participants should prepare, what materials to send and when, and whether declaration of interest forms have been collected, assessed and given management plans.

sections.title: Roles and process at the meeting

summary.text: Lists questions about roles and process at the meeting, such as the roles of each participant type, how conflicts of interest are presented and managed, and recording of deliberations. Gives separate question sets for meetings that finalize the scope and key questions and for meetings that develop recommendations, covering evidence summaries, evidence profiles, draft recommendations and templates.
Lists two questions on follow-up after the meeting: what follow-up occurs with participants, and how recommendations will be finalized if not completed at the meeting.

A numbered reference list for Chapter 3, citing items such as WHO declaration-of-interests and compliance pages, NICE materials, the Cochrane and Campbell collaborations, the review committee site and the WHO style guide.

sections.title: What is a guideline planning proposal?

summary.text: Defines a guideline planning proposal as a document outlining the rationale, scope, methods and resources of a proposed guideline, including protocol-like components plus information on contributing groups and administrative steps. States that the technical officer must submit one to the review committee for each guideline and that its approval is required for development to proceed to completion.

sections.title: What is the purpose of the planning proposal?

summary.text: Explains why a planning proposal is needed, giving reasons including securing early feedback on a credible guideline, setting its relationship to existing WHO guidelines, and avoiding overlap. Adds that it smooths the process by matching resources to scope, promotes accountability and protects integrity by fixing methods in advance and limiting bias.

Continues the reasons for a planning proposal, saying it makes development smoother and more efficient, promotes accountability through an agreed scope, methods and timeline, and above all promotes the integrity of the process. States that deciding methods in advance reduces arbitrariness and bias and that mid-stream method changes driven by findings or dominant members must be avoided.
States that the responsible technical officer in the leading technical unit develops the planning proposal; the sentence continues onto the next page.

Says the technical officer prepares the proposal in close collaboration with the steering group but must obtain broad input. Names the development group chair, the systematic review team, the methodologist and possibly the external review group as contributors to the key questions, and notes the group may meet in person, virtually or by email to define scope and methods.

sections.title: When should the planning proposal be developed and finalized?

summary.text: Explains the timing and preparation of the planning proposal, the first major product of development, starting when the unit decides to proceed and submitted once the key questions in the population, intervention, comparator and outcome format are complete. Describes submission to the review committee secretariat with a template and checklist after director approval, and presents a table of the essential proposal topics, from background and rationale to contributors, with responsible persons.

sections.title: What if there are major changes in scope or approach after the GRC has approved the planning proposal?

summary.text: Describes how to handle changes after the review committee approves the planning proposal, and lists the categories: major change in scope, change in packaging, major method change, change to a key question, and minor process changes. Says the first three kinds must be reviewed by the secretariat and sometimes the committee, while minor ones need not be, and the text includes the remainder of the proposal topics table covering writing, peer review, logistics, implementation and updating.

sections.title: For how long is an approved planning proposal in effect?

summary.text: States that the committee approves a planning proposal for six months beyond the planned publication date. Says delays beyond that should be discussed with the secretariat and that a revised proposal may be needed if the original methods and database searches could be compromised.
A reference list with one entry, the committee's intranet site.

sections.title: Reflecting WHO’s values in its guidelines

summary.text: The opening sentences of Chapter 5, stating that WHO's work aims to improve population health and decrease health inequities; the text breaks off mid-sentence.

Despite its heading, contains the end of the Chapter 5 introduction, saying that attention to these areas helps WHO deliver on its programme of work. States that the chapter describes how to integrate these considerations into each guideline development step through eight entry points.

Gives the background to the chapter, quoting the WHO Constitution on health and the right to the highest attainable standard of health and saying developers should consider how guidelines advance that right. Defines equity as unfair and avoidable inequalities and discusses measuring them, and begins describing human rights dimensions of the right to health, including its freedoms and entitlements.
A page containing only the number 47, under a heading for gender.

sections.title: Social determinants of health and health inequities

summary.text: Defines the social determinants of health and health inequities, and distinguishes gender from sex and describes how gender norms affect risk, access and outcomes. Explains how social determinants produce inequity and can be reduced through programmes and intersectoral action. Also reproduces a box of eight entry points for integrating equity, human rights and gender, from analysis of evidence on inequities to ensuring gender balance and accountability mechanisms in the guideline process.

sections.title: Eight entry points for integrating equity, human rights, gender and the social determinants of health into WHO guidelines

summary.text: Says WHO's guidelines must integrate equity, human rights, gender and social determinants and introduces the eight entry points as a practical approach, to be systematically considered although relevance varies by topic.

sections.title: Incorporating equity, human rights, gender and social determinants into each step in guideline development

summary.text: States that equity, human rights, gender and social determinants must be considered in all three phases of guideline development (planning, development, and publishing and updating) and in most steps within each.

Describes how to integrate equity, human rights, gender and social determinants into the planning phase. Covers the request for guidance, planning that aims to level up health across groups with stratifiers such as PROGRESS-Plus, composition of the contributing groups, and the planning proposal and scoping. Explains that the population, intervention, comparator and outcome elements of key questions should each take account of social position and the right to health.

Describes how to integrate these considerations into the development phase. Covers evidence retrieval and synthesis, including equity-focused reviews and tools, assessment of evidence quality on subpopulations where data are sparse, and formulating recommendations, where likely equity gains may support strong recommendations and sparse equity evidence may support conditional ones with a research agenda and monitoring.

Describes integration in the publishing and updating phase, saying the final guideline and derivative products must give clear messages on equity, human rights, gender and social determinants. Advises attention to language, examples, photographs and population descriptions from the start, and gender-sensitive, non-stigmatizing language in translations. The text ends at the heading for adaptation, implementation and evaluation.

Completes the guidance on adaptation, implementation and evaluation, warning that implementation can increase inequities and that WHO staff must monitor effects on equity, human rights and gender. Then lists the Chapter 5 references and opens Chapter 6, which defines the basic concepts and principles of declaring and managing interests and how staff collect declarations and manage conflicts.

sections.title: What is a conflict of interest?

summary.text: Defines a conflict of interest as a set of circumstances creating a risk that professional judgment about a primary interest is unduly influenced by a secondary interest, and gives WHO's declaration-form wording. Explains the terms primary interest, secondary interest and undue influence, and argues that a conflict exists whether or not it affects decisions, so phrases such as potential or perceived conflict should be avoided.

sections.title: What types of conflicts of interest exist?

summary.text: Distinguishes financial conflicts, which can be measured in money such as stocks, patents, commissioned work or honoraria, from nonfinancial ones, which are harder to identify and include professional advancement, prestige or drive to publish. Notes that intellectual conflicts of interest are one nonfinancial type.

Explains that declaring an interest does not automatically mean a conflict exists, and that a transparent and objective assessment is needed to decide whether one exists and manage it. Introduces the processes for identifying and managing conflicts during WHO guideline development.

sections.title: Why is a conflict of interest important in guideline development at WHO?

summary.text: Explains why conflicts matter, citing associations between secondary interests and study outcomes and conclusions, with evidence on guideline sponsors limited to case studies. States that conflicts can bias almost every step and undermine credibility of recommendations, guidelines and WHO, so developers must handle them in a proactive, transparent and defensible manner.

sections.title: What are WHO’s policies on conflicts of interest?

summary.text: Says guideline developers must know WHO's policies on obtaining declarations of interests and assessing and managing conflicts, points to an overview box and further web resources, and names the compliance, risk management and ethics office as a source of information.

sections.title: Who should complete a declaration of interests form?

summary.text: Explains who must complete a declaration of interests form: anyone providing independent advice in a personal capacity, including development group members, systematic reviewers, methodologists and the writer, who must also agree to publication of a summary. States that observers representing organizations need not complete one but their affiliations must be transparent. Presents a five-step overview of identifying, managing and reporting interests and a table of declaration and management by group, plus a figure of the assessment flow whose content is only yes and no labels.

sections.title: What interests need to be disclosed?

summary.text: Defines financial and nonfinancial interests that must be disclosed in guideline development and explains why they are assessed and managed. It lists examples of financial interests, such as paid work, research support, patents, grants and shares, notes the US$ 5000 reporting threshold (US$ 1000 for non-monetary research support), and gives examples of nonfinancial interests like prior publications, public positions and affiliations with advocacy organizations.

Describes how declarations of interests are collected using the standard WHO form, which must be completed, signed and assessed before invitations or contracts are issued. It adds that experts must report changes, that forms are confidential and securely stored, and that a curriculum vitae is requested alongside the form.

Sets out the three steps for assessing declarations of interest: staff review of the form with the expert's CV, a decision on whether a conflict of interest actually exists, and a judgement of how severe it is. It notes how little evidence exists on the effects of conflicts and that the guidance rests on best practice and expert opinion. It includes Table 6.2, with principles for collecting, assessing and managing declarations (report all funders, no private sector role, avoid and minimize conflicts, no financial conflicts for chairs), and Table 6.3, with criteria for judging severity such as the value and scope of the interest, the individual's discretion and the possible harm.

sections.title: Managing conflicts of interest at the individual level

summary.text: Explains that each declaration is reviewed by the responsible technical officer with the director of the technical unit, who decide case by case whether a conflict needs a management strategy. It stresses that disclosure alone is not adequate management.

Describes the options for managing a guideline development group member's conflict of interest, from no action, through restricted participation, to full exclusion. It lists conflicts that preclude participation, such as holding over US$ 5000 in shares or a patent on a product under consideration, and situations where participation should be limited, such as recent industry employment or authorship of key studies. It also states that no evidence supports a particular monetary threshold, so processes must be explicit, transparent and defensible.

Explains that declarations of interests are collected from all peer reviewers, although reviewers whose organizations clearly have a vested interest need only report their affiliation. It notes that reviewers with conflicts can still help anticipate controversy, but their declarations must be transparent and their comments assessed case by case.

sections.title: Managing conflicts of interest at the group level

summary.text: Explains that nonfinancial conflicts, including intellectual ones, may be managed at the group as well as the individual level because group composition influences recommendations. It cites evidence that physicians favour procedures they deliver and warns of committee stacking.

sections.title: Minimizing the risk posed by conflicts of interest when constituting guideline development groups

summary.text: Gives suggestions for constituting guideline development groups to limit the risk of intellectual conflicts. It covers chairs without financial conflicts (possibly a methodologist), a majority of members with no conflicts, balancing perspectives, separating the GDG from the evidence review and writing tasks, commissioning methodologists, and including varied stakeholders.

sections.title: Minimizing the risk posed by conflicts of interest during the guideline development process

summary.text: Describes ongoing responsibilities for managing conflicts during guideline development, including declaring institutional affiliations and presenting and updating declarations at each meeting. It then explains how declarations must be reported in the guideline (tabular or narrative, required for GRC approval), gives three worked examples of such reports, and states that forms are kept confidential for at least 10 years.

sections.title: What sources of funding are appropriate for WHO guidelines?

summary.text: States that WHO guidelines cannot be funded wholly or partly by private sector entities or non-state actors not at arm's length from them, and explains what counts as a private sector entity. It directs staff to make reasonable efforts to learn a funder's revenue sources and to consult the Office of Compliance, Risk Management and Ethics with questions.
A reference list for the chapter on declaration and management of interests, citing books, journal articles on conflict of interest and industry sponsorship, and WHO intranet documents.
Introduces the two basic types of questions, background and foreground, stating that background questions give context and rationale while foreground questions directly inform recommendations.

Defines background questions as those that supply context, such as definitions, disease prevalence and burden, or underlying mechanisms, and help frame the foreground questions. It gives examples, explains that they can usually be answered from a single cited valid source rather than a systematic review, and notes the exception where a prevalence question is central and becomes a foreground question.

Describes foreground or key questions as the basis of the evidence search behind recommendations, and explains how their focus varies by topic: efficacy, harms, acceptability, feasibility and cost for interventions; sensitivity and specificity for diagnostic tests; and baseline risk or relative risk for exposures. It illustrates each with example questions.
A near-empty fragment containing only the words Chapter 7.

Extraction put text under the wrong heading: this section ends the examples of foreground questions with a bedaquiline example for multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis. It then states that foreground questions are the most important for guideline development, usually need a systematic review with GRADE quality assessment, and should be framed in PICO format.

sections.title: Formulating key questions in PICO format

summary.text: Defines PICO as population, intervention or exposure, comparator and outcome, and mentions the PICOTS variant adding timing and setting. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the section.

Extraction put text under a heading that covers only part of it: it finishes the PICO introduction by noting that PICO also structures inclusion criteria and recommendations. It then lists guiding questions for the population element (demographics, setting, subpopulations) and for the intervention or exposure element (what treatment, policy or determinant is evaluated and at what levels).
A page number only, the number 81.

Lists guiding questions for the comparator element of PICO, covering alternatives such as standard practice, placebo, no intervention and other interventions, and stresses that comparators close to current practice are most useful. It also begins the outcomes element, asking which benefits, harms and equity effects matter most to affected people and calling for input from experts, programme managers and those affected.

sections.title: Examples of key questions in PICO format

summary.text: Presents six well-formulated key questions in PICO format, with the population, intervention, comparator and outcome labelled in each. It then contrasts one poorly formulated question about a drug for multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis, lists what it leaves unspecified, and gives a better rewording.

Explains that PICO can be applied beyond intervention efficacy to the main question types relevant to WHO guidelines: efficacy and effectiveness, harms, diagnosis, values and preferences, and risk assessment. It introduces Table 7.1, which gives the syntax and an example for each type.

Compares broad and narrow PICO questions, noting that broad ones give generalizable but resource-heavy and heterogeneous evidence while narrow ones are manageable but sparser, with the steering group able to split broad questions. It gives paired examples and shows, with a type 2 diabetes screening example, how several key questions can inform one recommendation question.

States that the number of key questions depends on guideline scope, resources and timeline, and that some recommendations need several key questions while others need one. It advises against combining several key questions into one because the workload stays the same.

Explains how to select and rate outcomes: the steering group drafts a list of desirable, undesirable and equity-related outcomes, the GDG adds to it, and members rate each on a 1 to 9 scale (7 to 9 critical, 4 to 6 important, 1 to 3 unimportant) from the perspective of those affected. It describes using the mean or median score, in-person discussion or a Delphi approach, and limiting the list to about seven important or critical outcomes.

sections.title: Finalizing the key questions and priority outcomes

summary.text: Says the steering group finalizes the key questions after input from experts and end-users, restricting systematic-review questions to areas of greatest controversy and uncertainty because they drive time and resources. It introduces the stepwise process shown in Figure 7.2.

sections.title: Step 1: generate an initial list of questions

summary.text: Describes step 1 of finalizing key questions: the steering group drafts an initial list of questions from the agreed scope and divides them into background and foreground questions.

sections.title: Step 2: draft the key questions in PICO format

summary.text: Describes step 2: the steering group, with input from the GDG, the systematic review team and the methodologist, writes the foreground questions in PICO format.
Describes step 3: the steering group lists relevant benefits and harms as outcomes, and the GDG reviews the list and may add important ones.

Describes step 4, in which the draft questions and outcomes are sent to the GDG and possibly other stakeholders for review and comment. The extracted text also contains the text of Figure 7.2, a flowchart of prioritizing key questions and outcomes for both foreground and background questions.

Describes step 5: the steering group, with input from the GDG, review team and methodologist, finalizes and ranks the background and foreground questions, after which it decides which foreground questions need systematic reviews.
Describes step 6: the GDG and other stakeholders, including those directly affected, rate or rank the listed outcomes using a formal process.

sections.title: Step 7: finalize the key questions and the important and critical outcomes

summary.text: Describes step 7: the steering group lists the high-priority key questions and the outcomes the GDG will use to formulate recommendations.

Explains analytic frameworks, which are diagrams showing how an intervention or exposure relates to the population, comparator and outcomes, and the pathways linking intermediate to distal health outcomes. It says they make evidence types and assumptions explicit and help explain GDG agreement and disagreement, and advises the steering group to develop them early, with input from the GDG, review team and methodologist.

A reference list of five sources for the question-formulation chapter, including GRADE, NICE guideline manual and US Preventive Services Task Force papers. The extraction also appends the opening paragraphs of the next chapter, which state that WHO recommendations must rest on the best available evidence and on a systematic review guided by key questions.

Defines a systematic review and explains that systematic reviews should underpin all WHO recommendations because they reduce bias and improve reliability. It lists seven characteristics of a systematic review, such as focused questions, explicit methods, predefined eligibility criteria, a comprehensive search and risk-of-bias assessment, and begins to note that non-systematic reviews lack these.

Continues from the previous section, stating that non-systematic and low-quality systematic reviews should not inform WHO guidelines and that staff must be able to recognize them. It distinguishes a systematic review from a meta-analysis, a quantitative pooling of outcomes, and says pooling studies not found through a systematic review should generally be avoided.

sections.title: Identifying and evaluating existing systematic reviews

summary.text: Explains that after scoping and drafting key questions, the next step is to identify at least one systematic review per key question, since existing reviews inform development whether or not a new review or an update is needed.

Describes where to find existing systematic reviews: comprehensive searches of databases such as Medline and EMBASE, with the limits of review-specific search filters, and searches of the Cochrane Library for reviews and protocols. It also covers how the GRC Secretariat can link staff to Cochrane, and names DARE, Epistemonikos and Health Systems Evidence as other sources.

sections.title: Is a new systematic review needed?

summary.text: States that a new systematic review is not always needed, since relevant, current and high-quality existing reviews should be used and updates are usually cheaper and faster than new reviews. The extraction also includes page-header text.

sections.title: Evaluating the relevance and quality of existing systematic reviews

summary.text: Explains how the steering group assesses existing systematic reviews for relevance (by comparing each PICO component with the guideline's key question), quality and timeliness before deciding whether a new review is needed. It names the AMSTAR, R-AMSTAR and Oxman and Guyatt checklists, warns against using them as scoring tools, and says there is no fixed rule for dismissing a review as out of date. The extraction includes the text of Figure 8.1, a yes-or-no decision flowchart.

sections.title: Steps in performing a systematic review

summary.text: Introduces the six basic steps of the systematic review process, distinct from the guideline development process, and says the steering group performs step 1 with input from the review team while the review team usually performs the rest in collaboration with the steering group.

sections.title: Step 1: develop and finalize the key questions and the studyeligibility criteria

summary.text: Describes step 1 of a systematic review: finalizing the key questions in PICO format and setting explicit study eligibility criteria, which are drafted and agreed by consensus between the steering group and the review team. It lists the additions to PICO for inclusion criteria, such as time frame, setting, study design, language and date range. The extraction also includes the text of Figure 8.2, which lists the six review steps.

sections.title: Step 2: identify information sources and search for originalarticles

summary.text: Describes step 2, designing and running the search for studies, which needs an information science expert, review of draft strategies and consultation with a WHO information scientist. It explains the trade-off between search sensitivity and precision and the need to search for studies from low- and middle-income countries, including regional databases under Global Index Medicus.

sections.title: Step 3: select studies and abstract data

summary.text: Describes step 3: screening records by title and abstract and then by full text against criteria set in advance, followed by extraction of data into predefined templates, with at least two people working independently. It also requires documenting databases, strategies, counts and exclusion reasons, and showing the flow of studies in a PRISMA diagram.

sections.title: Step 4: assess risk of bias of the individual studies

summary.text: Describes step 4: assessing the risk of bias of each included study, naming the main bias types (selection, attrition, performance and detection) and pointing to Chapter 9 for detail. It lists four instruments or resources, including Cochrane risk of bias tools and reports from Canadian and United States agencies.

sections.title: Step 5: synthesize and report the results and conclusions

summary.text: Describes step 5, synthesizing and reporting results, either as a meta-analysis when studies are sufficiently homogeneous or as a narrative synthesis when they are not. It explains that results go to the GDG with a GRADE confidence assessment, that meta-analyses give pooled estimates shown in forest plots, and that narrative methods and subgroup analyses should be specified in advance.

sections.title: Step 6: prepare the final report of the systematic review

summary.text: Describes step 6: reporting the review in the standard PRISMA format, with GRADE evidence profiles generally included. It says the level of detail may vary by purpose, but the report must make clear what was done and found without excessive study-level detail.

Explains how qualitative research can answer how and why questions, help interpret quantitative results, inform scoping, and illuminate barriers, facilitators, values, preferences and unintended social consequences. It points readers to the GRC intranet site and Cochrane resources for further guidance.

sections.title: Including other types of data in the systematic review

summary.text: Lists other data types that may be relevant to WHO guidelines, including mechanistic and animal studies for toxic substances, price and programme data or modelling for cost questions, surveys for values and preferences, and data on feasibility, equity and infrastructure.

Discusses updating an existing systematic review as a cheaper route to the needed evidence that is nonetheless complex and demands experience. It advises contacting the original authors, outlines difficulties such as missing information, outdated methods and unavailable data, and concludes that updating is reasonable when a high-quality, fully reported review using current methods exists.

sections.title: How to commission a systematic review

summary.text: Explains when and how to commission a systematic review, covering when a new review or update is needed, how cost depends on expertise, question complexity, literature volume and languages, and the use of Cochrane members. It lists five steps for the steering group, from a request for proposals to quality assessment, and requires commissioned teams to know GRADE and produce evidence profiles, with detailed terms of reference.

States that systematic reviews informing WHO recommendations must follow the standards in the Cochrane handbook, and that the Institute of Medicine standards give a useful list of elements of high-quality reviews.

States that the PRISMA reporting standards, including its equity extension, should be the basis for systematic reviews done for WHO guidelines and should be referenced in contractors' terms of reference.

A reference list of cited sources for the systematic review chapter, covering Cochrane and review-quality tools, databases, and reporting standards. The extraction also appends the opening of the next chapter, which introduces the GRADE approach used by WHO to assess evidence quality and lists public GRADE resources.
A divider for the evidence assessment chapter containing the heading, page numbers 109 and 110 and a running header, with no substantive text.

sections.title: What is the “quality of the evidence”?

summary.text: Defines the quality of the evidence, in GRADE terms, as the extent to which one can be confident that an effect estimate is correct, and in guideline terms as confidence that estimates are adequate to support a recommendation. It gives the alternative terms certainty of the evidence and confidence in the estimates of effect.

Explains that GRADE evidence profiles hold the quality assessment and a summary of findings for each important or critical outcome and key question. It says the GDG uses them as the basis for discussion, with outcomes in rows, brief judgements on quality factors and explanatory footnotes.

States that evidence assessment is a specialized task for a methodological expert experienced with GRADE, and that commissioned review teams must have this expertise. The extraction also includes Table 9.1, a GRADE evidence profile example on cryotherapy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, with its footnotes and very low quality ratings.

sections.title: What is the role of WHO staff in assessing the quality of the evidence?

summary.text: Describes the role of WHO staff in quality assessment: they must understand GRADE well enough to supervise commissioned work and advise the GDG, and in-house reviewers need in-depth knowledge. It also says GDG members should be briefed on evidence assessment before meetings, using online modules, publications or an introduction by the methodologist or GRC Secretariat.

sections.title: How is the quality of the body of evidence assessed for intervention studies?

summary.text: Explains that GRADE rates the quality of a body of evidence for each outcome as high, moderate, low or very low, not individual studies. It states that for intervention questions the starting point is study design, randomized trials versus nonrandomized and observational studies, and advises presenting different designs separately rather than pooling them in a meta-analysis.

sections.title: Five factors can lower the quality of the body of evidence for each outcome

summary.text: Explains that randomized trial evidence starts as high quality and observational evidence as low, and that five factors can lower the rating: study limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. It includes Table 9.2 defining the four quality levels, advises recording reasons for downgrading in footnotes without rating mechanically, and details the criteria for each factor, such as randomization and blinding for trials and confounding control for observational studies. It also covers how imprecision is judged by sample size and how publication bias is suspected and handled.

sections.title: Three factors can increase the quality of the evidence from observational studies

summary.text: Explains that observational evidence, low quality from the start, can be upgraded only if there is no reason to downgrade it, using three criteria: a dose-response gradient, a direction of plausible bias that would understate the effect, and a large magnitude of effect. It describes how precision and features such as rapid or consistent effects bear on upgrading, and says upgrades can be by one or two levels.

sections.title: How is the overall quality of the evidence determined?

summary.text: Explains how the GDG determines overall quality of evidence across all critical outcomes for a recommendation. The lowest quality among the critical outcomes sets the overall quality, with two exceptions where an outcome proves not to be critical or where higher-quality evidence on other critical outcomes already supports the recommendation.

sections.title: Is GRADE applicable in all situations?

summary.text: Considers whether GRADE applies in all situations, concluding that its structured, transparent framework has been used widely and that cases where it cannot be applied are rare and need a rationale approved by the GRC. It says GRADE also covers diagnostic tests, prognosis and baseline risk, while methods for environmental exposures, economic efficiency, network meta-analyses and modelling are still under development.

A reference list for the evidence assessment chapter, citing GRADE working group resources, the GRADE handbook and the GRADE guideline series in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, along with Cochrane risk of bias and inconsistency papers.

sections.title: Factors that determine the direction and strength of recommendations

summary.text: Names the four main factors that determine the direction and strength of a recommendation: quality of the evidence, values and preferences, the balance of benefits and harms, and resource implications. It begins a list of four further considerations that GDGs may discuss separately, starting with the priority of the problem.

Continues the list of additional considerations (equity and human rights, acceptability and feasibility) and says Table 10.1 sets out the GRADE criteria the GDG considers in turn to judge each factor's effect. The extraction mostly contains page numbers, running headers and the table's column headings.
States, as the first row of Table 10.1, that the quality of the evidence across critical outcomes informs recommendation strength, with higher quality making a strong recommendation more likely.

Gives the remaining rows of Table 10.1, describing how each factor affects the likelihood of a strong recommendation: values and preferences, balance of benefits and harms, resource implications, priority of the problem, equity and human rights, acceptability and feasibility. The text under the heading is the table body, which says that greater certainty, net benefit or advantage on each factor makes a strong recommendation more likely.

sections.title: Detailed criteria that should be considered when moving from evidence to recommendations

summary.text: Gives detailed guidance on the first two criteria for moving from evidence to recommendations. It explains that higher quality evidence favours a strong recommendation, and that values and preferences concern how people rate outcomes, can be gathered through reviews, primary surveys or GDG experience, and call for a conditional recommendation when uncertain or variable.

Explains that the GDG weighs the size of benefits and harms and the relative importance of outcomes, issuing a strong recommendation when benefits clearly outweigh harms and a conditional one when the balance is uncertain or the net benefit is small.

Explains that resource implications are normally included in recommendations and may be informed by formal economic evaluation, modelling or qualitative description. It says clearer advantages or disadvantages favour a strong recommendation, while uncertain costs favour a conditional one.
States that GDGs should be given evidence on burden of disease, baseline risk, prevalence or incidence, which matters especially when prioritizing across interventions.

Explains that GDGs must consider how an intervention affects equity and human rights, giving higher priority to those that increase equity, and that greater likelihood of reducing inequities and wider accessibility make a strong recommendation more likely.

Explains that lower acceptability of an intervention to key stakeholders makes a recommendation less likely or calls for an implementation strategy to address concerns. It lists what shapes acceptability, including who benefits, is harmed or pays, timing of effects and ethical or legal issues.

Explains that less feasible options, with greater implementation barriers, are less likely to be strongly recommended, and that feasibility depends on resources, programme factors, infrastructure and training.

Describes evidence-to-recommendation tables, which show how each factor informs a recommendation, improve transparency, focus discussion and record judgements. It says the GDG should at least document the four main factors and that the review team and methodologist can prepare much of the table beforehand.

Explains that recommendation strength reflects the GDG's confidence in the balance of desirable and undesirable consequences, with a strong recommendation issued when confident and a conditional (weak) one when uncertain. It refers to Table 10.2 as an interpretive aid.

Explains that strong recommendations convey confidence that desirable effects outweigh undesirable ones, are uncommon because the balance is rarely certain, and call for caution when evidence quality is low or very low.

Explains that conditional (weak) recommendations are made when the guideline group is less certain about the balance of benefits and harms, and that they usually state the conditions for implementing them. Includes a table interpreting strong versus conditional recommendations for patients, clinicians and policy-makers.

Describes how evidence-to-recommendation tables record the evidence, judgements and justification for a recommendation's direction and strength, along with subgroups, the formulation process, implementation issues and research gaps.

Describes how draft recommendations are prepared by the steering group or the guideline group and reviewed against GRADE evidence profiles and evidence-to-decision tables at the meeting. States that the group must agree on direction and strength by consensus, and that strong disagreement points to a conditional recommendation.

Sets out how recommendations should be written: clear, actionable, in PICO format, in the active voice, with consistent wording and an indication of strength and evidence quality. Advises on terms such as should and suggest, prefers explicit wording like recommending against over the ambiguous not recommended, and says each recommendation needs a justification, remarks on context and links to its supporting evidence.

Explains that a guideline group may occasionally decide the evidence is insufficient to make a recommendation, and gives a model statement for such cases. Stresses that this should be exceptional, that the lack of evidence must be stated openly, and that case reports or national experience can instead support a documented conditional recommendation.
Explains that significant evidence gaps should be described in the guideline with suggested questions and methods for future research, possibly prioritized and framed using PICO.
A reference list of publications cited in the chapter on developing recommendations, mostly on GRADE and moving from evidence to recommendations.

sections.title: What is a rapid advice guideline?

summary.text: Introduces the rapid advice guideline as an evidence-informed guideline produced within one to three months in response to a public health emergency, following the usual steps with modifications for the accelerated timeline.

Defines a rapid review as an evidence review using accelerated or modified systematic review methods, explaining that a standard systematic review can take six months to over a year and may be infeasible in an emergency. States that rapid reviews keep core values such as transparency and bias minimization, and lists efficiencies such as narrower scope, fewer outcomes, more reviewers in parallel and streamlined processes.

sections.title: What is the evidence on the validity and impact of rapid reviews and rapid advice guidelines?

summary.text: States that little guidance and few data exist on how rapid reviews perform against standard systematic reviews, and that approaches and reporting vary widely across organizations.

sections.title: Is a rapid advice guideline needed?

summary.text: Says the first question is whether a rapid advice guideline is appropriate in the emergency, as opposed to a standard guideline or deferring development, and that this should be considered at the planning stage.

sections.title: What is the type of emergency and the risk to public health?

summary.text: Explains how to examine the type of emergency driving the request, classing emergencies as natural, technological or conflict-related and sudden or gradual. Refers to WHO's rapid risk assessment manual and the Emergency Response Framework, including the grading of emergencies from Grade 1 to Grade 3.
Explains that a rapid advice guideline is mainly considered for a new situation or a known event in a new context, and that for non-novel events suitable high-quality guidelines may already exist.

sections.title: Does uncertainty need to be urgently addressed?

summary.text: Notes that rapid advice guidelines, like others, address uncertainty about what to do, and that the question is how quickly it must be resolved.

sections.title: What is the anticipated time frame for the event?

summary.text: States that rapid advice guidelines aim to give recommendations implementable within one to three months, and may be unsuitable if the event is expected to last beyond six months.

sections.title: Will the rapid advice guideline be rapidly implemented?

summary.text: Says a rapid advice guideline should be developed only if dissemination and implementation mechanisms exist and are feasible, considering health systems, acceptability, training and resources. Summarizes the conditions for going ahead: a clear need, manageable scope, adequate expertise and funding, and an implementation plan.

sections.title: How is a rapid advice guideline developed?

summary.text: Introduces the development of rapid advice guidelines as following the same basic steps as standard guidelines, with differences summarized in a table.

Advises the responsible technical officer to contact the Guideline Review Committee Secretariat early for guidance, help with the planning proposal and review team, and notes the committee must approve development at the planning stage for accelerated review.

sections.title: Formulate the various groups involved in guideline development

summary.text: Explains how to assemble the steering group, guideline development group and peer reviewers quickly, including expertise in ethical, social, legal, equity, gender and human rights issues. Presents a table of the steps of rapid advice guideline development across planning, development, and publishing and updating phases, naming who is responsible and the key points that differ from standard guidelines. Notes that human rights and gender issues often arise early in a response.

sections.title: Scope the rapid advice guideline and define the key questions

summary.text: Explains how to define the scope and PICO key questions once the need is established, noting such guidelines mostly address benefits and harms of interventions. Describes a rapid scoping search of sources such as MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library and existing WHO guidance, limited to one or two days and summarized in the planning proposal.

sections.title: Prepare the planning proposal for the GRC

summary.text: Explains that a rapid advice guideline still needs a planning proposal submitted to the review committee, in the same format as for standard guidelines. Says it should be detailed, kept up to date as a living document with rationale for changes, because the rapid review process is more fluid and documentation supports transparency.

sections.title: How do rapid reviews compare with systematic reviews?

summary.text: Contrasts rapid with standard systematic reviews: restricted search criteria, existing systematic reviews as first evidence, targeted iterative screening, less emphasis on meta-analysis and shorter reports, while keeping transparency and explicit methods.

Describes four types of rapid review, from a full systematic review done quickly to reviews of only systematic reviews and guidelines, or of primary studies, and refers to a figure outlining their features.

sections.title: Steps in the rapid review process
Select the types of evidence to be collected and identify the appropriate sources

summary.text: Explains which evidence to target and where to look, emphasizing existing high-quality systematic reviews and guidelines, then primary studies, landmark papers and good observational studies as needed. Notes that rapid reviews usually search only two to three key databases.

Explains how to build rapid review search strategies, using subject headings and text words, with review by a team member, content experts and an information specialist. Notes that study-design filters can surface top evidence first and that a rapid review may favour precision over recall, with the choice reported.
Advises that a limited grey literature search, such as checking relevant organizations' websites, may be considered, in consultation with a WHO library information specialist.

Discusses common eligibility restrictions for rapid review searches, especially language limits chosen by topic, illustrated by an Ebola protective equipment review limited to English and French. Says restrictions must be documented in the proposal, report and guideline, and that titles in excluded languages should be listed in an appendix.

sections.title: Other strategies for identifying relevant literature

summary.text: Describes other ways to find evidence, such as real-time data collection like the survey of repatriated health workers during the 2014 Ebola outbreak, and scanning reference lists. Includes a box of common search restrictions covering sources, language, accessible studies, grey literature, dates and region.

Describes screening and study selection for rapid reviews as following standard methods, with two people independently screening titles and abstracts and two reviewers assessing full texts, reaching consensus with a third reviewer if needed. Notes that one reviewer plus a check of exclusions is an acceptable alternative at the first step.

sections.title: Use a stepwise approach with emphasis on higher levels of evidence

summary.text: Recommends starting with evidence from systematic reviews and adding primary studies only when justified in the planning proposal and reflected in timelines and budget. Acknowledges that restricting by outcomes risks selective reporting bias but is a trade-off under time limits.

Explains that records not available electronically are generally excluded because of time, though WHO information scientists should be consulted first and abstracts may still help when evidence is sparse.

Describes data extraction for rapid reviews: extract only information the guideline group needs, use a pilot-tested form, and have a second reviewer verify, or check a random sample of at least 10 percent.

sections.title: Assess the risk of bias at the individual study level

summary.text: Explains that risk of bias should be assessed for individual studies and may help select studies for inclusion. Describes evidence synthesis for rapid reviews, with a PRISMA flow diagram, a narrative summary organized by PICO, stepwise extraction of effect estimates, outcome-specific synthesis, and meta-analysis only if time allows while reporting existing meta-analyses.

sections.title: Assessing the quality of the body of evidence using GRADE

summary.text: Explains that the quality of evidence for each outcome should be assessed with GRADE, focusing on critical outcomes, and that narrative syntheses can also be graded. Notes that modifications to standard methods can be listed under other considerations, and includes a figure on four approaches to rapid review of evidence, from summarizing one high-quality systematic review to updating one or adding primary studies.

Describes the concise rapid review report, which should allow replication, note evidence gaps and carry a disclosure that it is not a gold standard systematic review. Lists suggested components in a box covering introduction, methods, results, discussion, information page, references and appendices.

sections.title: Convene the meeting of the guideline development group

summary.text: Explains that the meeting of the guideline development group must be planned from the start, covering venue, invitations, declarations of interest and travel, which needs dedicated administrative support. Notes that virtual meetings are possible but an in-person meeting is generally preferable.

States that the GRADE approach and its tools apply to rapid advice guidelines, noting it is seldom feasible to collect primary data on values, preferences or resource use, though readily available data such as costs should be gathered.

Says the drafting of a rapid advice guideline needs the same process and resources as a standard one, with the writer, usually the technical officer or steering group member, or a contractor, identified early.

Explains that rapid advice guidelines still need accelerated, abbreviated peer review by three to six key individuals and leading external organizations, perhaps with 48 to 72 hours to respond. Says that in rare cases no peer review is possible, in which case all relevant WHO departments must at least be able to give input.

sections.title: Implementation and the importance of context

summary.text: Explains that research evidence often comes from settings unlike the emergency, so contextual factors, barriers and facilitators must be considered, the synthesis tailored to the local context, and decision-makers given what they need to apply it.
States that publishing a rapid advice guideline follows the same steps as for a standard guideline, with electronic dissemination first and print as needed locally.

Explains that rapid advice guidelines must be kept up to date as new data emerge, and that their short lifespan and review-by date should be shown prominently. Discusses deciding when to replace one with a standard guideline, using the 2009 H1N1 guidance on pregnant women as an example, and notes WHO may sponsor systematic reviews to confirm high-impact recommendations.

sections.title: Guideline Review Committee processes for rapid advice guidelines

summary.text: Describes the Guideline Review Committee's role: it must approve development of a rapid advice guideline, judging appropriateness through the planning proposal, and review the final guideline. Says the handbook's principles still apply with case-by-case exceptions, and that the committee provides expedited reviews and ad hoc meetings.

Concludes that rapid advice guidelines are developed in one to three months with a very narrow scope, early engagement of experts and the review committee Secretariat, and more fluid evidence review methods. Stresses that core principles of minimizing bias, transparency and meeting audience needs still apply, and that limitations and a commitment to update must be stated.

A reference list of publications and WHO documents cited in the chapter on rapid advice guidelines, followed by the opening lines of the next chapter on producing and publishing the guideline, which begin a list of what needs coordinating.
A short fragment of bullets continuing a list (following WHO production and publication processes, disseminating and updating the guideline), filed under a peer review heading.

Describes the required guideline format: an executive summary with key recommendations, strength and evidence quality, a main body with introduction, methods, recommendations, conclusions and participant and interest details, and appendices for supporting documentation. Also covers use of PRISMA and the AGREE-II appraisal before clearance, and begins the peer review section, stating that WHO guidelines must undergo peer review by the external review group and WHO departments, with changes limited at that stage. Text under this heading therefore extends into the next section.

Lists ways to involve external reviewers earlier, such as circulating systematic review protocols, lists of included studies and draft evidence profiles, and states that all guidelines need external peer review, with a few reviewers and short turn-around for rapid advice guidelines.
Introduces the guideline production process, which follows the same steps as other WHO publications, with details on the staff intranet and a brief overview given here.

Advises identifying a writer early, whether staff or freelance, estimating time and fees, with guidance on rates and a week for 5000 words. Recommends avoiding multiple authors, since unpaid chapter drafts tend to create more work.
Advises that guidelines should avoid naming proprietary products, describing devices and diagnostics generically and consulting WHO legal counsel if in doubt.
Advises engaging an editor and proofreader from lists kept by the publishing office, and booking them early because the best are reserved months ahead.

sections.title: Executive clearance and approval by the Guideline Review Committee

summary.text: Says the Guideline Review Committee reviews final guideline documents as part of executive clearance, after the relevant director's approval and before the assistant director-general.

Describes the layout and printing steps after executive clearance: using external typesetters or the graphics team and existing templates, then obtaining a cover, ISBN and barcode. Explains that the publishing office arranges printing quotes and print runs and that the proofreader should check the printer's proofs.

Explains that dissemination means making guidelines accessible, advertising them and distributing them, with priced distribution through sales agents and the bookshop and mandatory free distribution to bodies such as libraries and country offices, to be planned with the publishing office.
Advises producing at least a web-ready PDF of the guideline, possibly with HTML and extra materials, and consulting the WHO web team.
Describes archiving requirements: departments send the final electronic file to the WHO Library repository, or regional office library, with a printed copy for the print collection if produced.

Explains that translations, particularly into the six official languages, should be planned and budgeted, with experts checking technical content. Notes that translating only executive summaries can cut costs and that the meaning and strength of recommendations must not change.

Explains that the commissioned systematic reviews and the guideline's process or recommendations may be published in journals, within open access and copyright policy, and that external publications with WHO authors require internal clearance.

Advises planning a dissemination strategy early, using launches, press releases, web announcements, regional distribution, stakeholder endorsement and mobile applications, and preparing shorter derivative products such as charts and manuals.

Explains that guidelines should carry a review-by date showing how long recommendations are expected to stay valid, set by considering the pace of research, questions without evidence and the potential need for new advice.

States that recommendations not developed under the handbook's standards, especially those predating the review committee's 2007 creation or ignoring equity, human rights and gender, should be updated. Advises prioritizing controversial areas or those with new evidence, and discussing incremental updating with the committee Secretariat.

sections.title: Guidelines that are near or beyond their “review-by” date

summary.text: States that technical units are responsible for examining guidelines for currency as the review-by date approaches and planning updates where recommendations may need changing.

sections.title: Recommendations that may be out of date

summary.text: Explains that early updates should be based on the total body of evidence through a new or updated systematic review, and that changing recommendations requires committee review while adding evidence alone does not. Says stakeholders should be told when recommendations may be invalid and updates are planned.
A reference list of publications cited in the chapter on producing and publishing the guideline, including PRISMA, AGREE II and papers on when guidelines should be updated.

Describes how adaptation, implementation and evaluation should be considered during development, including tools and resources for countries and partners who will lead adaptation. Explains adaptation to local circumstances at regional, national or subnational level and that implementation is context-specific and the responsibility of national or subnational groups, supported by WHO offices through promotion, workshops, tools and coordination. Section text begins mid-sentence because extraction dropped the chapter's opening heading.

Explains that monitoring and evaluation assess a guideline's effectiveness and impact, and that guidelines should include performance measures such as dissemination, adaptation, policy changes, knowledge, practice, health outcomes and equity, and costs. Recommends baseline measures, implementation research and a specific set of indicators with disaggregation.
A reference list with two items, on the multicountry evaluation of Integrated Management of Childhood Illness and the ADAPTE manual for guideline adaptation.
